hero.name: Omkar
hero.who: a 19-year-old college kabaddi player in Kolhapur who keeps choosing comfort over training

story.b: Omkar plays kabaddi for his college team in Kolhapur, and the district selection trials are three months away. His coach wants the team at the ground near Rankala lake by five thirty every morning. Omkar knows this. His alarm rings at five, he presses snooze, and the November cold keeps him under the blanket. Most days he reaches the ground at six fifteen, if he goes at all. At night he has a second plate of misal with his friends. When he loses a raid in practice, he snaps at his teammates. His coach tells him talent is not his problem. Omkar knows exactly what he should do. He just keeps choosing the easy thing instead.

ask.q: Omkar knows exactly what he should do but keeps giving in. What is the most useful place to start?
o: Wait for a burst of motivation closer to the trials
Watch videos of great players to feel inspired
Start with small physical choices he controls daily, like getting up on time
ask.why: Motivation comes and goes, and inspiring videos feel good without changing his mornings. Discipline is built through repeated small choices, and the body is the simplest place to practise. Getting up when the alarm rings is a daily vote for self-control.

chapters.take: Discipline is not a feeling you wait for. It is a choice you practise.

story.b: Omkar moves his alarm clock to the shelf across the room, so he has to stand up to switch it off. His rule is simple: once he is standing, he does not sit back down. He splashes cold water on his face, pulls on his track pants and walks out before his mind can start arguing. The first week is brutal. His legs ache and the lake path is dark and freezing. By the third week, getting up is still hard but no longer a battle. He also notices something he did not expect. It has become easier to say no to the second plate of misal and to put his phone away at night.

ask.q: Omkar's alarm rings on a freezing morning and his body begs for ten more minutes. What should he do?
o: Snooze once, since ten minutes will not matter
Get up at once, before he starts arguing with himself
Skip the morning and train double in the evening
ask.why: One snooze teaches his mind that comfort wins the argument, and evening plans often fall apart too. Getting up immediately, before the debate begins, is the small physical win that trains self-control. Each morning he does it, the next one gets a little easier.

chapters.take: Win the first small battle of the day, and others follow.

story.b: After practice, the team always rushes off for vada pav and leaves the mats in a crooked heap. Omkar used to rush off too. One evening he stays back and rolls every mat properly and stacks them straight. Nobody asks him to. He starts doing other small things with care. He washes his own kit and laces his shoes the same way every time. He writes his training log neatly in a notebook instead of scribbling it. He submits his college assignments on time. In drills, he finishes every footwork pattern fully instead of cutting the last few short. Within a month, his coach notices that his ankle holds have become sharper and cleaner.

ask.q: After practice, the team rushes off and leaves the mats in a messy heap. What should Omkar do?
o: Roll and stack the mats properly, even if nobody is checking
Leave them, since mats have nothing to do with winning
Tell the junior players it is their job
ask.why: How he handles small chores reflects how he handles everything, including the last tired repetition of a drill. Skipping it because nobody watches trains carelessness, and passing it to juniors avoids the work. Doing small things properly builds the habit of doing all things properly.

chapters.take: How you do small things shows how you will do big ones.

story.b: Now fired up, Omkar swings to the other extreme. He trains twice a day, every day, with no rest. He refuses every sweet, even his mother's Diwali chakli and karanji. He sleeps late because he is doing extra core work at night. By the third week his body feels heavy, his raids are slower and his left knee aches whenever he climbs stairs. His coach pulls him aside and tells him he is not being disciplined, he is being reckless. Omkar listens. He shows the knee to the college physiotherapist, who asks him to ease off and come back in a week. He takes one rest day every week and eats a small bowl of faral with his family.

ask.q: Omkar has been training twice daily without rest and his knee aches. What is the wisest move?
o: Push through, since tough players ignore pain
Stop training completely until the trials
Ease back, add rest days, and have the knee checked by a physio or doctor
ask.why: Discipline is not doing as much as possible. Pushing through pain can turn a small problem into a serious one, and stopping completely throws away his fitness. Training in moderation, resting and getting the knee checked by a professional keeps him strong for the long run.

chapters.take: Too much of a good thing is still too much. Find the middle.

story.b: In a practice match against a rival college, Omkar makes a clean raid and returns to his half. The referee, a senior player, gives the point to the other side. The old Omkar would have shouted and kicked the mat. This time he feels the heat rise in his chest, and he counts slowly to ten while walking back to his line. The opposing raider grins at him. Omkar keeps his face still. On his next raid he scores two points, quietly. After the match, when everyone has calmed down, he asks the referee politely about the call. The referee admits he was unsure. Omkar walks home feeling stronger than after any workout.

ask.q: In a match, an opponent mocks Omkar after a failed raid. How should he respond?
o: Shout back so the opponent knows he cannot be pushed around
Stay calm, breathe, and put his focus into the next raid
Ask the coach to take him off before he loses control
ask.why: Shouting hands the opponent exactly what he wanted, a rattled player. Asking to come off avoids the moment rather than mastering it. Keeping his composure and focusing on the next raid is the harder, more disciplined choice, and it usually wins more points too.

chapters.take: Staying calm under pressure is discipline too, often the hardest kind.

story.b: Omkar's roommate Vishal is also on the team, and he still skips most mornings. Each day, leaving the room in the dark, Omkar feels the urge to wake him and give him a speech about commitment. He has even rehearsed it. One morning he catches himself feeling superior and stops. Discipline is something he chose for himself, not something to force on others. So he just goes, quietly, every day. He leaves his spare torch on Vishal's table. When a junior drops an easy catch in practice, Omkar pats his back instead of glaring. Two weeks later, Vishal is standing at the door at five fifteen, yawning, asking if he can walk with him.

ask.q: Omkar's teammate Vishal still skips morning practice. What should Omkar do?
o: Keep his own standards quietly and invite Vishal along without judging him
Lecture Vishal every night until he changes
Complain to the coach so Vishal gets punished
ask.why: Discipline is a standard Omkar sets for himself, not a stick for others. Lectures and complaints make Vishal defensive and hurt the team. A quiet example and a kind invitation leave the door open, and people often follow what they see more than what they hear.

chapters.take: Be strict with yourself and generous with others.

story.b: On the morning of the district trials, Omkar wakes at five, before the alarm. He does not feel like a different person. He feels like someone who has got up on time for twelve weeks. He laces his shoes the usual way, eats a light breakfast and walks to the bus stand with Vishal. In the trial match, a selector makes a strange call against him. Omkar breathes, walks back and raids again. His knee holds up, thanks to the rest days. A week later the list comes out and his name is on it. That evening, after practice, he stays back and rolls the mats. Vishal and two juniors stay back to help.

chapters.take: Daily self-control, practised quietly, slowly shapes who you become.
